Afreen, come, sit on the step. You're cross with that boy in your class because he copied once, and now even his cricket is "bad"? Let your Jagdish chacha from next door tell you something.
When I was nine, in our school near Hisar, I saw Bhola peep at another boy's slate during a sums test. From that day he could do nothing right for me. His clay bullock at the school fair? Ugly, I said. When he shared his roasted chana at lunch, I thought he wanted something. When he helped me carry water, I told myself he was showing off.
Years later I saw that bullock again, kept on his mother's shelf. It was beautiful. I had simply stopped looking at him.

qa.a: Afreen could look at each thing on its own, like asking whether the cricket shot was actually good, instead of letting the copying decide everything.

qa.a: Bhola may have felt confused or hurt, since he kept sharing and helping and still got nothing warm back, without knowing one test was the reason.

In Class 9, our maths teacher called me "the sleepy one" in the first week, because I yawned during the register. I'm Thomas, and that name followed me for a year.
When I finished a whole page of algebra, she said, "Someone must have helped the sleepy boy." When I forgot my compass once, the whole class heard about it. My friend Noor once swapped our notebooks as an experiment. Same answers, my handwriting copied by Noor. Noor's version got "Excellent." Mine, the week before, got "Late again?"
I stopped raising my hand. What was the point? It felt like she was only looking for the mistakes.
It changed in Class 10, with a new teacher who didn't know the name. By December I was answering again.

qa.a: She called him "the sleepy one".

qa.q: What change turned things around for Thomas, and why did it help?
qa.a: A new teacher in Class 10 who didn't know the name judged his work fresh, so he felt seen again and started answering by December.

qa.q: How might Noor see the notebook experiment?
qa.a: Noor probably found it unfair and a little shocking that the same answers got 'Excellent' for Noor and 'Late again?' for Thomas, and may have wanted to prove it to Thomas.

grounding: A teenage boy labelled early as sleepy finds his good work ignored and small slips noticed, showing how a label limits what others see.

qa.a: Karthik probably felt pushed out after apologising, which may explain why he stopped offering, even though he understood the survey better than anyone.

The shipment labels for the Busan warehouse had gone out with the wrong postcodes, and two pallets came back. Soo-ah, the logistics lead, found Leila's initials on the label file. By lunch she had half-typed a message moving Leila off the Friday export run.

The monthly stock count at the district hospital pharmacy came out wrong by forty boxes of bandages, and the sheet had Lalit's signature on it. Nandita, the pharmacy in-charge, felt her jaw tighten. Santosh, the senior storekeeper, leaned in her doorway. "Lalit again? Put him back on night inventory."
Nandita almost nodded. Then she caught herself: "again" was one mistake in eight months, and she had been ready to decide on it alone.
"Give me an hour," she said.
She pulled out Lalit's previous counts. Every one matched. She walked to the store room and found the answer on the wall calendar: that day, a delivery had arrived during the count, and Lalit had been called away twice to sign for it.
At the staff meeting she said, "We stop the count while deliveries come in." Lalit, who had been staring at the table, looked up.

Last month, before my dance recital, I was so sure I knew what kind of friend Payal was. I'm Indu, and I'm fifteen. Payal had promised to sit in the front row. The chair I'd saved for her stayed empty. Afterwards I sent her a long message, all capitals at the end, and she didn't reply for three days.
In those three days I decided everything. She was jealous. She only cared about her new friends. I even told my cousin that Payal "was always a bit selfish."
Then her reply came: her family had moved house that week, the internet at the new flat wasn't working, and her phone had gone in a box that got lost in the shifting. She'd only just found it.
What bothers me now is how quickly I built a whole person out of one empty chair, and how I never once thought of a move, a box or a dead connection.

qa.q: How long did Payal take to reply to Indu's message?
qa.a: She didn't reply for three days.

qa.q: Why did deciding that Payal was jealous feel so reasonable to Indu at the time?
qa.a: Indu was hurt by the empty chair, and with no reply, explaining it by Payal's character felt more certain than imagining things Indu could not see.

qa.q: If Indu faced another silence like this, what could Indu try before deciding?
qa.a: Indu could list a few everyday reasons a friend might go quiet, like a move or a broken phone, and wait or ask gently before telling anyone what the friend is like.

qa.q: How might Payal feel when she finally reads the long message ending in capitals?
qa.a: Payal would probably feel sad and a little defensive, having missed the recital because of a chaotic move, and then finding herself judged for it.

grounding: It shows a teenager deciding a friend who did not reply was uncaring, without thinking of circumstances such as a move or a lost phone.

On the fourth floor of a Gurugram insurance office, Pankaj's claim files came back from audit with missing signatures for the third week running. "He's just sloppy," someone said at the coffee machine.
Hrithik, who sat opposite him, wasn't so sure. Pankaj had been leaving at exactly six every day lately, which he never used to, and answering calls in the stairwell.
So Hrithik asked, simply, over lunch: "The audit keeps flagging your files. Is something making the afternoons hard?"
Pankaj hesitated. "My father's been unwell. I do the files in a hurry before I leave to take him to appointments. I didn't want to make excuses."
"That's not an excuse. It's a reason," Hrithik said. "And the signatures are still a problem. Want to try doing the signature pass first thing in the morning?"
Pankaj nodded, looking relieved and a bit embarrassed at once.

qa.a: For the third week running.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik feel unsure about calling Pankaj sloppy?
qa.a: Hrithik had noticed Pankaj leaving at exactly six every day and taking calls in the stairwell, which suggested something might be going on.

qa.q: How did Hrithik handle both the reason and the problem?
qa.a: Hrithik accepted that Pankaj's father being unwell was a real reason, while still treating the missing signatures as a problem and suggesting a morning signature pass.

qa.q: What would change for Pankaj if Hrithik had just agreed with 'he's just sloppy'?
